blocks.text: Daniel Orkleson held the telephone receiver against his ear and waited through another ring.
Luke floated beneath the lip of the pay phone's metal hood, keeping out of sight of the sidewalk. He had already counted enough rings to know Eleanor was not coming.
“Perhaps she's upstairs,” Daniel said.
“Then she'll miss you again.”
Daniel pressed the receiver harder against his ear.

A bus stopped at the corner. Through the glass side panel, he watched people step down and scatter along the pavement. He turned his face toward the telephone, pulling the collar of his stained lab coat higher.
The ringing continued.
blocks.alt: Daniel waits at a public pay phone in his stained lab coat while bodyless Luke hovers beneath its metal hood, watching skeptically.

blocks.text: “You could leave a message,” Luke said. “Oh, wait. You need somebody to answer.”
Daniel put the receiver down.
“She's busy.”
“She said no.”
“People reconsider.”
“Has she?”
Daniel checked the coin return. He put what he found into his pocket and stepped away from the phone.
Luke followed above shoulder height, close to the wall. A woman coming out of the corner shop glanced toward them. Daniel kept walking. Luke slipped behind him before she could get a second look.
They took the narrow passage between two buildings and came out behind a row of shuttered shops. The loading recess they had used the night before was still empty.
Their cardboard had been moved.
Daniel stopped. Two flattened boxes lay beyond the shelter of the overhang, wet at one corner. He dragged them back beneath it and prodded the dry edge with his shoe.
“Somebody's been here.”
“Yes,” Luke said. “Probably somebody who owns it.”
Daniel sat on the driest piece. The concrete behind him was cold through his coat. He had tried folding the coat underneath himself the night before, but then his arms had been cold instead.
“This is temporary.”
“You said that yesterday.”
“It was temporary yesterday, too.”
Luke hovered in front of him. A drop fell from the overhang and struck the pavement between them.
Daniel shifted his foot away from it.

He had spent the morning thinking about a hot meal. He disliked the way this kept interrupting everything else. Whenever he tried to consider equipment, he remembered the smell coming from the bakery they had passed.
He felt through his pockets. A crumpled wrapper, a pencil worn short enough to disappear between two fingers, a few coins. He counted the coins again.
Luke watched.
“She isn't going to give you any more.”
“I heard you the first time.”
“I don't think you heard her.”
Daniel closed his hand around the money.
For a while, neither spoke. A truck backed into the next yard. Its reversing beeper stopped, and somebody rolled up a door.
Daniel leaned forward to see whether the driver was looking their way.
“We should move before they start asking questions.”
“Where?” Luke asked.
“I'll think of somewhere.”
“When?”
Daniel looked up sharply.
Luke did not move away.
“You said you could finish your work. You said you needed the boy. Then you needed Flaming Head. Then you needed more equipment.”
“I did need more equipment.”
“And what do you need now?”
Daniel opened his hand. The coins lay in his palm.
blocks.alt: Seated on cardboard in a loading recess, Daniel shows his remaining coins while Luke confronts him about his broken promises.

blocks.text: Luke's iron teeth shifted with a small scrape.
“I kept helping you.”
“I know.”
“I carried you out of there.”
“I know that, too.”
Daniel's answer came too quickly. He looked down at the money again.
Luke lowered until they were almost eye to eye.
“You keep telling me what you'll do when we get somewhere else. We're somewhere else now.”
Daniel could see his own enormous glasses reflected faintly in the metal jaw.
“This isn't a laboratory.”
“No.” Luke looked at the wet cardboard. “It isn't.”
Daniel put the coins away. He wanted a bench, a lamp, paper that had not been folded around somebody's lunch. He wanted one conversation in which Luke did not ask a question he could not answer.
“I can't work here,” he said.
“Then stop telling me you're working on it.”
The truck driver came around the corner carrying a clipboard.
Daniel got up before the man could speak. He left the cardboard where it was.
They walked until the shops grew busier. Daniel took the quieter side of the street, keeping near the buildings. Luke moved above him, using signs and projecting doorways to stay out of the open.
At the next corner, a folded newspaper lay on a bench beside an empty coffee cup.
Daniel glanced up and down the street before picking it up.
“If you're looking for her number,” Luke said, “you already know it.”
Daniel shook the paper open.
He had meant to check whether his photograph was in it. He had learned to turn those pages inward before carrying a newspaper anywhere.
A small picture near the bottom made him stop.
It showed a machine on a stand. Beside it were two photographs of the same piece of equipment, with a ruler laid along the base of each.
Daniel brought the paper closer to his glasses.
“What?” Luke asked.
Daniel did not answer. He turned the page toward the light.

The Army was bringing an experimental shrinking device to Cleveland. A public demonstration was planned for the following week. The report described equipment reduced for transport, then restored to its original size.
Daniel read the paragraph again.
blocks.alt: Daniel excitedly studies a newspaper announcing an Army demonstration next week, while Luke hovers beside him with a doubtful expression.

blocks.text: Luke descended behind the back of the bench. “What is it?”
“Look.”
He held the paper where Luke could see the photographs.
“A small machine,” Luke said.
“The same machine.” Daniel tapped the larger photograph, then the smaller one. “Before and after.”
Luke looked more closely.
“They can make it small?”
“And bring it back.”
Daniel read to the end of the article. He went back to the beginning, checking the announcement, the description, the mention of accompanying Army equipment.
The cold in his coat bothered him less.
“Think what you could carry,” he said.
Luke looked at the paper, then at him.
“A workbench. Machinery. An entire set of instruments.” Daniel's finger moved down the column. “Take them somewhere private, restore them, and there they are. Ready to use.”
“You'd still need somewhere to put them.”
“Somewhere empty. There are places.”
He turned the paper sideways to examine the photograph of the display equipment.
“A tank,” he said.
Luke stared at him.
“You could put a tank in your pocket.”
“What would you do with a tank?”
“Do you know what's in one? Engines. Electrical equipment. Parts I couldn't buy even when she was paying.”
He stopped, glanced toward the street and lowered his voice.
“Restore it wherever you need it. Take what you want. Move the rest.”
Luke watched Daniel fold the newspaper, keeping the announcement on the outside.
“You're going to steal it.”
Daniel looked offended that he had said it quite so plainly.
“They're displaying it,” he said. “We can find out how it works.”
“That wasn't what I said.”
“I heard you.”
Luke rose until his eyes were level with Daniel's again.
“Does it give me my body back?”
Daniel's grip tightened on the paper.
“It gives us somewhere to start.”
“I had somewhere to start before I came to you.”
A car passed. Daniel waited for its engine to fade.
“With a properly equipped laboratory, I can do research again. Real work. I can't do it on a piece of cardboard.”
Luke said nothing.
Daniel smoothed a crease across the announcement with his thumb.
“Next week,” he said. “We only have to manage until then.”

He was already reading the details again. Luke could see the change in him: shoulders lifted, eyes moving quickly behind the thick lenses, one finger following a sentence as if it were a line on a diagram.
Daniel tucked the newspaper beneath his coat.
“Come on. We need to look at the place.”
He set off toward the corner.
Luke stayed beside the bench for a moment. He had heard that voice before. Usually there had been a switch or a locked door at the end of it.
Daniel looked back.
“Well?”
Luke could have gone over the roofs. For a moment he looked up at them.
Then he followed, keeping the newspaper and his uncle in sight.
